title: Norway holds at 4.25% as the inflation surprise tests the case for another rise
summary: Norges Bank’s committee voted unanimously on 12 August to hold the policy rate at 4.25%. Underlying inflation had undershot its projection by enough to warrant waiting, yet members saw little change in several forces that had sustained inflation. June’s assessment had pointed to a likely increase at a forthcoming meeting. In August the governor still saw a possible need to raise rates. There was no new forecast. The path reaching just above 4.5% at year-end, with inflation returning to 2% in 2029, belonged to June’s projections and was conditional on policy evolving along that path. September’s forecasting round would give the committee an opportunity to revisit it. (Monetary policy statement and opening of the committee deliberations.)

The surprise was greater beneath the headline. In July, twelve-month headline inflation of 3.0% was broadly as projected, helped upwards by electricity prices and distribution charges. CPI adjusted for tax changes and excluding energy products, CPI-ATE, came in at 2.7% for the second consecutive month, 0.6 percentage points below the July projection. Food, beverages and ICT equipment accounted for much of the slowdown, although other goods and services also contributed. The committee’s average of alternative underlying measures had fallen less and remained higher than CPI-ATE. The governor’s chart showed both headline and adjusted inflation still above the 2% target. Norges Bank’s combination of short-term forecasting models had revised down its projections for coming quarters. Members nevertheless had little new wage information; earlier labour-cost increases could continue feeding through to prices. Years of above-target inflation also raised the risk of households and firms planning on its persistence. (Deliberations, inflation and policy stance; presentation, slide 3.)

Energy and the currency offered limited grounds for changing that medium-term judgement. The committee reported considerable summer oil-price volatility and continued constraints on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. By the meeting, spot and futures oil prices were close to June levels, while gas and freight costs were somewhat higher. Imported price pressures overall were broadly as expected. The import-weighted krone had recovered from an earlier weakening to around the level assumed in June. Members discussed whether the exchange-rate pass-through used in their analysis could help explain the import-price surprise. Short-term market expectations for Norwegian policy rates had fallen somewhat since June, whereas foreign policy expectations had edged up. The committee reported that markets still priced in tightening in Norway during the autumn; it supplied no meeting-specific probability. (Deliberations, international economy and inflation.)

The domestic cost of further tightening was more apparent in housing than in aggregate employment. Registered unemployment was 2.1% in July, in line with the June forecast. Survey unemployment was also broadly stable over the summer, at a distinctly higher level on slide 4. Retail sales and vehicle registrations pointed to consumption expanding broadly as assumed. Existing house prices, however, fell 1.1% on a seasonally adjusted basis in July, and some members worried that lower prices would further depress already weak construction. In its separate capital-buffer decision, the committee left the countercyclical buffer at 2.5%. Banks reported broadly stable lending standards and households and firms retained ample access to credit, even as developer profitability and debt servicing were under pressure. For the rate decision, this combination left room to observe whether the inflation undershoot would persist while avoiding further restraint on a vulnerable sector. (Deliberations, activity and monetary policy stance; countercyclical capital buffer decision.)

The capital-buffer assessment gives an additional check on the source of financial restraint. Twelve-month household credit growth had stabilised around 4.7% in 2026. Household debt had generally grown more slowly than income in recent years, with the largest declines in debt-to-income ratios among the most indebted. That improvement had begun to slow. Rising real wages still supported debt servicing, while non-interest-bearing credit-card debt reached a summer high and total consumer-debt growth was roughly in line with the same period in 2025. A record on one card balance measure was therefore insufficient evidence of a general acceleration in indebtedness. Secondary-market turnover had fallen during the summer but remained high in level, while the market for new homes was weak. Each of these distinctions matters when inferring spending pressure from one housing or credit series (capital-buffer assessment, household debt and housing).

Norwegian companies’ credit premia had risen after the Middle East conflict began, then receded to near their ten-year average. Bond-market activity recovered before summer. Banks saw little change in aggregate credit standards and expected little change in the third quarter. Risk was concentrated more specifically among property developers, whose profitability and ability to service debt had suffered and whose bankruptcies had increased. Commercial property sale prices had levelled off, and few new office completions were expected, supporting rents in areas such as central Oslo. Banks still reported low losses, strong profitability and capital and liquidity above requirements. These observations help explain the simultaneous choices to retain restraint through the policy rate and to leave the countercyclical buffer at 2.5%. The stated reason to lower the buffer would be a downturn that substantially reduced, or threatened to reduce, credit supply. Weak developer activity alone did not demonstrate that condition (capital-buffer assessment, access to credit, property exposures and bank resilience).

questions.question: How much of the July inflation miss should change the medium-term rate path?
questions.detail: The committee distinguished a substantial CPI-ATE miss from a smaller move across alternative measures, and it had little new wage evidence. Persistence would matter more for the case for another increase than a reversal in a few product categories. Compare the next available Statistics Norway component releases and wage indicators with the June projections, paying particular attention to labour-intensive domestic services and the breadth of price increases.

questions.question: Had Norwegian short rates already absorbed the change in the committee’s language?
questions.detail: Market pricing had eased since June but still included autumn tightening. The report gives neither the probability attached to each meeting nor the move specifically attributable to the announcement. For an investor in short-dated Norwegian rates, compare timestamped pre-announcement and post-announcement NOK money-market quotes, the relevant fixing conventions and contemporaneous foreign-rate moves before attributing a repricing to Norges Bank.

questions.question: Could weakness in housing spread to employment or credit supply?
questions.detail: July’s house-price fall and weak construction concerned some members, while banks reported ample credit availability and aggregate unemployment changed little. A broadening downturn could increase the cost of another hike and affect developer credit differently from bank funding. Examine housing starts, construction employment, developer arrears and the next bank-lending survey, distinguishing borrowers seeking less credit from lenders tightening terms.

questions.question: Were developer losses beginning to change the supply of credit elsewhere?
questions.detail: Compare developer bankruptcies and bank loss provisions with senior bank funding spreads, loan approval standards and lending to firms outside property. A decline in new homes or loan applications could reflect weak demand alone. A broader tightening of standards accompanied by rising funding premia would have different implications for both the capital buffer and the effect of another policy-rate increase.

limitation: The note covers the published decision, deliberations, capital-buffer decision, governor’s prepared remarks and slides. The Norwegian-language press-conference video and its Q&A are outside this reading.
